title: Relations between optical spectral parameters and the (far-)infrared continuum in Type~1 active galactic nuclei
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: This study combines multi-wavelength continuum data with optical spectral properties for a far-infrared (FIR)-selected sample of Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) from AKARI data. We explore the relation between AGN physics and concomitant star formation processes using empirical correlations of optical and multiwavelength data. We measured spectral parameters including full widths at half maximum (FWHMs) and velocity shifts of broad and narrow optical emission lines, as well as continuum luminosities from GALEX FUV to AKARI 160 microns. The sample contains 88 AGNs observed at both optical and FIR wavelengths. About 50% are Seyfert 1s with both broad H$β$ and H$α$ lines; almost all remaining objects are S1.9s with only broad H$α$. The FWHMs of broad H$β$ and H$α$ are anti-correlated with luminosity in most bands. Shifts of narrow H$β$, H$α$, and [O III] 5007 lines and FWHM of [O III] 5007 correlate with optical and IR luminosities. Luminosities at 65 and 90 microns are more strongly connected with optical and other spectral properties than those at 140 and 160 microns. These trends extend the well-known Eigenvector 1 (EV1) correlations into the MIR and FIR domain. The anti-correlation between broad-line FWHMs and NIR and MIR luminosities is probably caused by the inclination of the torus and accretion disc: higher inclinations see less AGN radiation. However, most objects fall into Population A along the quasar EV1 main sequence, where narrower broad H$β$ profiles and FIR excess emission are commonly linked to higher Eddington ratios.

title: The Magnetized Universe: From planet-forming disks to the high-redshift universe
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) is magnetized at all scales and phases in our Galaxy and other galaxies across the Universe. Spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations are essential to probe the role of the interstellar magnetic fields in the dynamics of the cold universe, and how this affects the star formation process, and planet formation in nearby star forming regions. Such observations are also essential for understanding magnetic fields in active stars and the shaping and evolution of the circumstellar environments of evolved stars. While ALMA has been revolutionary in advancing our knowledge about magnetic fields in the ISM, the limitations in calibration, especially for circular polarization, and sensitivity for large samples, have hindered robust measurements of field strengths, which are essential for fully assessing their role in ISM dynamics. An ALMA2040 that broadens spectro-polarimetric capabilities to include robust circular calibration and increases sensitivity with more collecting area will enable crucial observations of magnetic fields across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales to fully ascertain the influences of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to forming planets.

title: Survey of Orion Disks with ALMA (SODA) IV: Millimeter variability of protoplanetary disks
comment: Accepted by A&A on 12/10/2026
summary: Context. Short-term millimeter-wavelength variability in Class II young stellar objects (YSOs) has been considered minimal, often dismissed as very rare in ALMA-based studies on short timescales. However, recent findings suggest that variability on sub-day timescales is significant. Aims. This study aims to quantify short timescale (~1 hour to ~3 days) millimeter flux variability in unresolved Class II YSO disks observed as part of the SODA survey, leveraging its large dataset to assess the statistical significance of such variability across the LDN 1641 and LDN 1647 regions in Orion. Methods. We analyze ALMA Band 6 observations of 873 YSOs obtained over multiple epochs using a custom flux extraction pipeline to separate individual execution blocks. By computing variability factors and statistical deviations from the mean flux, we identify sources exhibiting significant variability, accounting for noise and calibrator stability. Results. Even with conservative selection criteria, we identify 20 variable sources within the sample (~5.3% of all detections). The maximum of the measured variability factor is >=7 over about one hour. More liberal selection criteria yield up to 60 sources that could be called potentially variable (~15.9%). Conclusions. The number of variable sources detected in our sample indicates physical processes operating on time scales of hours, likely associated with magnetic reconnection and/or synchrotron radiation or strong cases of magnetic accretion changes. These detections show the need to reconsider typical stability assumptions in single-epoch observations and calls for follow-up studies in star-forming regions with ALMA. Masses derived from unresolved measurements could potentially be biased by this sort of variability.

title: The coordinated radio and infrared survey for high-mass star formation - VI. Higher-resolution follow-up of point-like northern ultra-compact H II regions
comment: 24 pages, 12 figures
summary: The CORNISH survey provided the most complete sample of ultra-compact H II (UCHII) regions in the northern Galactic plane to date, but at its 1.5 arcsec resolution the most compact, and plausibly youngest, members of the sample could not be morphologically classified. We present Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) A-configuration observations at 10 GHz of 69 such CORNISH UCHII regions, reaching an angular resolution of ~0.2-0.3 arcsec and a typical rms noise of ~10 microJy/beam. All but two of the imaged targets are detected; the two non-detections lie in fields that are dynamic-range limited by bright neighbours. Six targets (~9 per cent) are resolved into pairs of sources, and a further 15 CORNISH UCHII regions detected within the fields reveal complex, multi-component structure. We also report candidate massive young stellar object (MYSO) jet knots and a row of three compact sources coincident with a previously unresolved infrared-dark H II region. The targets have a median deconvolved angular diameter of ~0.9 arcsec and physical diameters of 0.004-0.17 pc (median ~0.03 pc), with no correlation between angular size and distance, consistent with a population of intrinsically compact, young regions. Spectral indices between 1.4 and 10 GHz place ~32 per cent of the targets below the thermal free-free limit, possibly indicating non-thermal emission or variability. These data enable morphological classification of nearly the entire CORNISH UCHII sample, which will be presented in a forthcoming paper.

title: Gaia in Technicolor. I. A Simple Variability-Encoded Color-Magnitude Diagram
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific
summary: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram is one of the most important tools in stellar astrophysics. In its modern, empirical form as the Gaia color-magnitude diagram (CMD), each star is represented with a point determined from its time-averaged brightness and color. However, many stars are intrinsically variable, and the fixed-point representation ignores the variety of ways in which a star can vary. As a system pulsates, eclipses, is irradiated, erupts, or otherwise varies, it moves through the CMD along a trajectory whose size, slope, and shape are determined by the physics driving the brightness and color variability. Here we exploit the near-simultaneous, three-band, multi-epoch photometry (MEP) released for ~11.7 million sources in Gaia DR3 to construct a variability-encoded CMD (VECMD). In this updated take on the traditional CMD, each star is represented not by a point but by a linear segment approximating the path it traces in absolute magnitude and color as it varies. Because these trajectories are built from the raw epoch data, they are agnostic to period and do not require phase-folding. We show that radial-mode pulsators trace looped, Lissajous-like trajectories that can encode the phase lag between radius and temperature. The Hertzsprung bump is even visible in the CMD loops of some Cepheids. Variable binary systems can trace tight color-correlated lines and/or hooked paths. Accreting and dust-obscured systems trace long, high-amplitude tracks aligned with the outburst or reddening vector. Distinct regions of the VECMD are dominated by distinct trajectory morphologies. We argue that these trajectories are period-independent fingerprints well suited to machine learning classification, which we will pursue on the much larger epoch-photometry sample expected in Gaia DR4. Finally, we present a free app called IVECMD for finding, classifying, and analyzing variable stars in the VECMD.

title: Characterizing the Martin Luther King Event: Sun to Earth Evolution of the January 19, 2026 Geomagnetic Storm
summary: We present a comprehensive Sun-to-Earth analysis of the extreme space weather event of 18 -19 January 2026, hereafter the Martin Luther King (MLK) storm, which produced a severe (G4) geomagnetic storm and one of the most intense solar radiation storms of Solar Cycle 25. The geomagnetic disturbance was driven by a fast Earth-directed coronal mass ejection (CME) associated with an X1.9-class flare from NOAA Active Region 14341. We combine multi-viewpoint remote-sensing observations, in situ measurements from Solar Orbiter and Wind, and physics-based magnetohydrodynamic simulations using the CORHEL-CME framework to reconstruct the eruption from the low corona to 1 au and identify the mechanisms governing its geoeffectiveness. Observations and simulations indicate that the eruption originated from a right-handed magnetic flux rope embedded in a complex magnetic environment dominated by a neighboring positive-polarity coronal hole. The simulations reproduce the observed CME morphology, asymmetric expansion, magnetic fields measured at both spacecraft, and Dst index evolution. The main discrepancy is attributed to filament material not included in the model. Favorable magnetic polarity alignment between the CME and coronal-hole field minimized magnetic erosion through interchange reconnection, enabling rapid escape and preservation of the strong southward magnetic field that drove the geomagnetic storm. The prolonged recovery phase resulted from interaction between the trailing CME and a following high-speed stream from the same coronal hole. These results demonstrate that storm intensity was primarily established by the coronal magnetic configuration, whereas storm duration was controlled by the ambient solar wind.

title: Milky Way Near Twins (MWNeTs). II. Applications of a Hierarchical Framework to NGC 3521, NGC 2903, UGC 11487, and CGCG 047-026
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 3 Tables, submitted to A&A
summary: Galaxies resembling the Milky Way in present-day global properties may have followed different evolutionary histories. The Milky Way Near Twins (MWNeT) framework introduced in Paper~I addresses this through seven successive stages of present-day compatibility and evolutionary diagnostics. We apply this framework to NGC~3521, NGC~2903, UGC~11487, and CGCG~047-026, spanning different levels of observational completeness and outcomes within the hierarchy. We combine archival measurements with analyses of galaxy structure, spectral-energy-distribution similarity, atomic-gas profiles, and optical nuclear diagnostics. Stages~I--IV assess environmental, structural, nuclear, and global compatibility; Stages~V--VII examine SEDs, rotation curves, and evolutionary fingerprints. We distinguish supported compatibility, partial agreement, measured incompatibility, and unconstrained diagnostics. We jointly assess these four galaxies within the MWNeT framework for the first time and derive new structural, SED-comparison, and H\,{\sc i} profile measurements for UGC~11487. NGC~2903 is a well-constrained benchmark, whereas NGC~3521 combines extensive evolutionary information with uncertain bar identification. UGC~11487 has a securely detected bar, quantitative UV--IR SED similarity, and distinctive transient nuclear tracers, but its nominal stellar mass lies below the adopted interval and its extended rotation curve remains unconstrained. CGCG~047-026 meets the initial environmental, structural, and nuclear-state criteria but remains largely unconstrained at higher stages. The four applications demonstrate the framework's ability to organise complementary evidence and identify observational priorities without equating missing data with physical incompatibility. They establish a basis for future systematic searches and for using candidate near twins as external laboratories of Milky Way evolution.

title: The START mission: Probing the 2029 Apophis Flyby via a Low-Cost Geocentric SmallSat
summary: The Student-led Threatening Asteroid Reconnaissance of Tsinghua (START) marks the inaugural mission of the Tianxing Program, a deep-space exploration initiative led by students at Tsinghua University. Conceived as a low-cost, rapid-response small-satellite mission, START will investigate the near-Earth asteroid (99942) Apophis during its close approach to Earth in April 2029, when significant terrestrial tidal forces will offer a rare opportunity to observe the physical and dynamical response of a rubble-pile asteroid in real time. The 300 kg spacecraft is scheduled for rideshare launch into low Earth orbit in early 2028 and will then use solar electric propulsion to transfer to a circular mission orbit with a semimajor axis of approximately 38,000 km and an inclination of 55 degrees. START will execute a high-speed flyby of Apophis from a closest distance of 7 km at the asteroid's closest approach to Earth, to capture its tidal response. The payload suite consists of a high-resolution narrow-field camera, a wide-field navigation camera, and three near-infrared multispectral imagers. By acquiring centimeter-scale imagery and meter-scale reflectance spectra, the mission will characterize the asteroid's surface morphology and composition and monitor immediate tidally induced surface modifications. Ultimately, START will provide geometrically complementary, high-cadence datasets to international flagship missions to Apophis, demonstrating a highly scalable and cost-effective architecture for future planetary defense and small-body exploration.

title: Flashing with colours: Photometric indicators of an early interaction in type II supernovae
comment: 29 pages, 19 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present early-time optical photometry and spectroscopy for a sample 27 previously unpublished type II supernovae (SNe II) observed by the Precision Observations of Infant Supernova Explosions (POISE) collaboration, combined with a literature sample of 59 events to form a total sample of 86 objects. The resulting light curves comprise near-daily cadence, percent-level precision $uBgVri$ photometry. From spectra acquired within four days of the estimated explosion time, transient narrow emission lines of highly ionised elements, referred to as `flash features', can be identified. Based on the presence or absence of these lines, the SNe were categorised. We estimate key photometric properties, including rise times, peak absolute magnitude, and colour evolution. Our tests indicate that flash SNe are, on average, more luminous at the peak than their non-flash counterparts, which is consistent with previous studies. Interestingly, statistically significant differences were found in the rise times in the $B$ band, with flash SNe exhibiting a tail towards longer rise times. Flash SNe are generally bluer than non-flash events, with distinct colour distributions at 20 days post explosion, likely reflecting intrinsic differences rather than host-galaxy extinction. Colour-curve breaks within 30 days of explosion provide a clear separation between flash and non-flash SNe. The change in slopes across the break, combined with the absolute peak magnitude, yield a strong diagnostic of the flash-spectroscopic properties. This indicates that photometric observations alone may be used to identify SNe experiencing an interaction with dense circumstellar material, even in the absence of early-time spectroscopy.

title: Inferring the delay time distribution of type Ia supernovae with CAALAM I: SED modelling choices and their effect on the delay time distribution
comment: 16 pages, 18 figures, Submitting to A&A
summary: A delay time distribution (DTD) quantifies the lag between progenitor formation and the subsequent explosive event. The DTD for a sample of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) from a survey can be modelled through relative rates and the star formation histories (SFH) of all individual galaxies. Modern wide-field surveys require computationally efficient methods to model the DTD without modelling large samples of non-host galaxies. We model the DTD for a volume limited sample from SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility. The aim is to study the effect of varying SED modelling assumptions, including stellar templates, dust attenuation, SFH models, and photometric coverage. We present a new modelling framework, the Conditional Astral Ancestry Latency Analysis Machine (CAALAM), to infer the DTD of a sample of SNe Ia from the posterior of their host galaxy SFH. A model consisting of a standard stellar template, a non-parametric SFH and a flexible dust attenuation law, is favoured by the data and predicts a non-parametric DTD peaking at 100-330 Myr. When modelled as a power law, the DTD has a characteristic exponent of $-1.30 \pm 0.04$. The exponent is sensitive to dust attenuation, photometry, or SFH. When the DTD is convolved with the SFHs of the host galaxies, we find a bimodal progenitor age distribution, with $\sim60\%$ of progenitors with ages around 1.1-3.6 Gyr and the remaining progenitors older than 3.6 Gyr. We show a correspondence between the modes of the distributions of SN Ia light curve stretch and the progenitor ages. Our inferred DTD implies that most SNe Ia ($\sim 60\%$) occur promptly within 330 Myr of progenitor formation. However, the implied progenitor ages from the DTD convolved with the SFHs from our sample are significantly older. This suggests that the DTD might be a mixture of a prompt and an extended progenitor channel.

title: Extended J-band spectroscopy of red supergiants: parameter identifiability and metallicity robustness
comment: Comments: 20 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Red supergiants (RSGs) provide a near-infrared metallicity diagnostic complementary to optical hot-supergiant spectroscopy, but their low-resolution extragalactic use requires tests of parameter identifiability and modelling robustness. We quantify the information content of extended J-band RSG spectra at R=2000 over 1.155-1.340 um and assess recovery of effective temperature, surface gravity, microturbulence, and metallicity. Using MARCS/TURBOSPECTRUM spectra and an emulator, we perform a six-node Fisher analysis and controlled mock experiments, and analyse 21 SpeX spectra of 20 RSG candidates towards Per OB1. All four parameters produce measurable responses, but only 8-10% of the raw metallicity information and 4-7% of the gravity information are independent of the other parameter directions. Extending beyond 1.22 um provides median fractions of 60% of the raw and 66% of the nuisance-orthogonal metallicity information. Gravity dominates the weakest Fisher mode, while its prior choice shifts association means by at most 0.03 dex. Matched mocks recover metallicity with an rms error of 0.04 dex. Standard continuum treatment biases solar-metallicity mocks by about -0.23 dex, reduced to about -0.01 dex by our adopted treatment. Plausible CNO mismatch adds a zero-point sensitivity of 0.04-0.05 dex, and regularised covariance changes association means by at most 0.03 dex. The preferred analysis gives a mean [Z] = -0.10 dex with a star-to-star dispersion of 0.09 dex. Extended low-resolution J-band spectra therefore yield recoverable metallicity and temperature constraints once continuum placement and weak parameter directions are controlled, although the absolute scale remains conditional on the adopted atmosphere and line-formation framework.

title: Pathfinder results for populations of planet-forming discs with SKA
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures. Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026, ArXiv:2026.20366). Report No. AASKAII/Greaves01 Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances which will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Imaging of few-millimetre-sized dust grains (pebbles, on the construction path to planets) in protoplanetary discs has begun. The Planet-Earth Building-Blocks Legacy e-MERLIN Survey is a unique pathfinder for SKAO, imaging a sample of disc-host stars around 4.4 cm wavelength at 55 - 120 mas resolution. PEBBLeS has surveyed 10 flux-ordered fields of the northern sky, and the L1448C-N and HL Tau systems are presented as examples. The prospects for extending this science with SKAO are bright, including shorter integration times and better sensitivity to fainter outer discs. Simulations are presented of how a southern analogue to the HL Tau disc could look to SKA-Mid AA* in bands 5a and 5b. The initial lack of long baselines is suggested to pose a significant risk for imaging of planet-related features in protoplanetary discs.

title: Comparing Infrared & X-ray-selected Active Galactic Nuclei host galaxy star formation rates to the galaxy main sequence
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: A key method of exploring the relationship between active galactic nuclei (AGN) and their host galaxies is to determine the astrophysical properties of galaxies that host AGN, and compare them to those that do not. Star formation rates are believed to be strongly related to nuclear activity, both indirectly via their common fuel supply, and directly via the energy injected by the AGN either suppressing or enhancing star formation. Strong observational evidence of a direct link between nuclear activity and in-situ star formation has proven elusive, likely in part due to the very different timescales of nuclear activity and episodes of star formation. To overcome these challenges, some studies have demonstrated that evidence of the aforementioned link may be found in the distributions of AGN power and star formation rates. While previous attempts to determine these distributions have largely focused on X-ray-selected samples of AGN, in this study we also attempt to determine the star formation rate distributions of infrared-selected AGN. The results vary between our samples, but at low redshift (0.8 < z < 1.2) we find that more powerful X-ray-selected AGN are more likely to occur in galaxies with higher specific star formation rates, consistent with previous studies. At higher redshifts (1.0 < z < 1.8), this trend is reversed with higher power AGN tending to occur in galaxies with lower specific star formation rates. By contrast, infrared-selected galaxies at 1.0 < z < 1.8 show no evidence of a changing star formation rate distribution with AGN power.

title: A Neural Network - Based Tool for Rapid Orbital Solution of Contact Binary Systems
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables, accepted by ApJ
summary: With the rapid growth of large-scale time-domain surveys, vast amounts of photometric and spectroscopic data are continuously being released. A substantial number of contact binaries have been identified, accompanied by both light curves and radial velocity observations. Traditional modeling of these datasets relies on computationally intensive physical models, which limits their applicability to large-scale analyses. To this end, this paper proposes the use of a fully connected neural network and a SIREN (Sitzmann et al. 2020) model to rapidly generate radial velocity curves. After training, the models can rapidly generate radial velocity curves with high accuracy, significantly reducing computational costs and enabling efficient large-scale studies. This method was further integrated with the light curve computation framework developed by Li et al. (2025), allowing simultaneous fitting of radial velocities and light curves. To assess the reliability of the proposed model, synthetic observational datasets were constructed and used for parameter estimation. The deviations between the derived parameters and the ground-truth values were analyzed quantitatively, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the model's accuracy.

title: The environments forming stellar and planetary systems
comment: 10 pages + 1 page affiliations, 1 figure, ALMA2040 whitepaper
summary: How does a star's birth environment set the mass, angular momentum and chemical complexity delivered to its planet-forming disk, and thereby whether it builds planets, brown dwarfs or stellar companions? This requires following material from the cloud to the sub-au to few-au scales where infalling gas, magnetized winds and the disk interact, across all star-forming environments. At frequencies where young disks are optically thin, current facilities, even ALMA after its Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade, fall short by a factor of a few in angular resolution and an order of magnitude in sensitivity. Likewise, resolving how disks around distant high-mass stars fragment into tight multiples requires a linear resolution of a few to a few tens of au, currently out of reach. Yet the disks characterized so far lie almost exclusively in nearby, isolated clouds at near-solar metallicity, although the environment (radiation field, ionization rate, gas and stellar density, pressure and metallicity) varies by orders of magnitude across the Galaxy. Most stars, probably including the Sun, form in clustered regions at kpc distances, and the widest metallicity range lies farther still, in the outer Galaxy, the Central Molecular Zone and the Magellanic Clouds. With three times finer angular resolution and ten times the sensitivity, ALMA2040 will follow the path of material from cloud to disk across the full stellar-mass spectrum and, for the first time, measure how this path changes with environment: resolving the sub-au infall-impact and wind-launching zones nearby, disk fragmentation and the onset of multiplicity in distant high-mass regions, and disk formation at a few tenths of solar metallicity. It will thereby reveal the dust-obscured, embedded origins of planetary systems that optical and infrared facilities, including the ELT, see only once they emerge, and show how the birth environment shapes them.

title: Broad Line Regions behind a Haze II: A Three-dimensional Electron-scattering Model of the Broad Br$γ$ Line in NGC 3783
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, accepted by ApJ
summary: We investigate the broad Br$γ$ line in the type-1 active galactic nucleus NGC 3783 using three-dimensional Monte Carlo electron-scattering radiative transfer with SKIRT. Paper-I reproduced the observed smooth core and broad wings by convolving an intrinsic Keplerian profile with the analytic electron-scattering kernel of Laor (2006). Here we instead transport photons through explicit source and scattering geometries. For a partially covered Keplerian source, three-dimensional transfer broadens only the scattered photons and leaves an unscattered double-peaked core. For the thin Keplerian source motivated by Paper-I, a comparison of four scattering-geometry classes shows that neither a disk-like scatterer nor the tested halo variants reproduce both the core and wings. We therefore construct a two-component-source (2CS) model containing an inner Keplerian source disk, a rotating disk haze, a nearly spherical halo haze, and direct emission from a slower outer disk. A reference 2CS calculation gives Xi^2 =1.154 at i=15 deg. Polar cones with an input radial optical depth tau_hole=0.1 preserve the line profile and give a measured Thomson-thin sightline. The preferred low redistribution width, full-column ionization, and weak recombination emission cannot all be realized by a uniform thermal halo. The 2CS model is therefore a physically motivated parametric description whose medium must ultimately be tested with self-consistent radiative transfer, ionization, and dynamics.

title: Contrasting geometries of kiloparsec-scale stellar flows associated with giant Galactic cavities
comment: 40 pages, 4 main figures and 5 Extended Data figures; Supplementary Information included
summary: Giant bubbles and cavities are widespread in star-forming galactic discs, yet the stellar dynamics associated with such structures remain poorly constrained. Here we combine Gaia Data Release 3 with three-dimensional extinction information to identify 3,502 massive-star candidates corresponding to initial masses $M_{\rm ini}\gtrsim8\,M_{\odot}$ within 5 kpc of the Sun. A search of the stellar-density field alone, independent of interstellar-medium morphology and stellar kinematics, reveals two prominent overdensities, R1 and R2, with characteristic scales of approximately 1.3 kpc. Both are subsequently found to be associated with previously identified giant interstellar cavities in projected position and line-of-sight location. After subtracting locally fitted background velocity fields, stars with full three-dimensional velocities reveal coherent divergent in-plane motions across both structures. R1 extends well beyond a known massive-star association and exhibits strongly anisotropic expansion, with one principal strain rate robustly positive and the other consistent with zero. R2 instead exhibits positive strain rates along both principal directions, indicating broadly two-dimensional internal expansion. These results show that density-selected, cavity-associated stellar structures of comparable scale can host coherent kiloparsec-scale flows with contrasting internal flow geometries and need not share a common stellar kinematic organisation.

title: Isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction kinetics of HCO+ and HOC+
comment: accepted in A&A
summary: The HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio has been observed to vary significantly in different astrophysical environments, making it an important diagnostic tool for exploring the interstellar medium. However, uncertainties in the reaction rates and branching ratios of key chemical reactions involving these ions affect the conclusions drawn from observations of either these species or other species that are derived on their basis. Here, we present isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction rate coefficients of reactions involving HCO$^+$ and HOC$^+$ using a cryogenic ion trap experiment. We measured the rate coefficients of the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ with H$_2$ and CO, as well as three different reactions producing both isomers: CO$^+$ + H$_2$ , H$_3^+$ + CO, and ArH$^+$ + CO. Our results show that the reaction of CO$^+$ with H$_2$ predominantly produces HCO$^+$ with a negligible yield of HOC$^+$ . This result is in agreement with recent theoretical predictions, but in major contrast to the generally accepted branching ratio based on previous experimental results. We also find that the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ is efficient with both H2 and CO. We were able to assess the impact of our new measured reaction rate coefficients on the predicted HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio using a state-of-the-art astrochemical model.

title: MIDSSAR: MId Dispersion Spectrograph for Stellar Activity Research
comment: 16 pages, 22 figures. Accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: We have developed and commissioned MIDSSAR (MId Dispersion Spectrograph for Stellar Activity Research), a novel fiber-fed, dual-band spectrograph optimized for high-cadence monitoring of stellar superflares and magnetic activity phenomena, mounted on the 3.8-m Seimei Telescope at Kyoto University Okayama Observatory. Utilizing a custom-designed volume phase holographic grating and a commercially available volume binary transmission grating, the instrument achieves simultaneous observations of key chromospheric activity indicators: the CaII H&K band (382.5-406.5nm) at a resolving power of R=13,800, and the H$α$ band (641.1-667.6nm) at R=18,200. MIDSSAR is strategically integrated with the existing high-dispersion spectrograph GAOES-RV to enable concurrent photosphere-chromosphere monitoring. The control software coordinates high-speed dual-camera exposures down to 1ms while incorporating real-time telescope telemetry into the data headers. We also developed a dedicated data reduction pipeline that automatically executes calibration, spatial reconstruction of the 61-fiber bundle, and one-dimensional spectral extraction with a wavelength precision of $\sim$ 0.002nm. Initial on-sky test observations conducted from March to May 2026 successfully verified the system's quantitative readiness. The observed signal-to-noise ratio characteristics perfectly align with modeled theoretical limits under varying seeing conditions, confirming that the entire instrument complex successfully meets its primary design requirements and operational expectations for systematic stellar astrophysics surveys.

title: A precessing AGN with S-shaped morphology discovered in MALS
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present J1221$-$1354, a precessing AGN discovered in the MeerKAT Absorption Line Survey (MALS) using deep L-band (0.9--1.6\,GHz) radio data. Its `S'-shaped morphology, revealed by the excellent surface brightness sensitivity of MeerKAT, is consistent with jet precession. Ancillary optical and infrared data establish the source as a Type 2 AGN in a moderately overdense environment. The approaching (southern) jet is brighter but shorter than the receding jet, with the northern edge of the receding jet showing a significantly younger spectral age. These features are peculiar, but consistent with a jet reorientation event in an asymmetric ambient medium, in which the jet re-enters a cavity of previously deposited plasma. A simple ballistic model yields a precession period of $P=290\pm30$\,Myr, consistent with geodetic precession in a supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) with a binary separation of less than 1.1\,pc. We expect that deep radio continuum surveys in the near future will uncover many more such systems, helping to further strengthen the connection between jet precession and SMBHBs, and the latter's implications for the gravitational-wave background detected with pulsar timing arrays.

title: $N$-body simulations of the open cluster M67 -- I: global cluster properties
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: The most recent Gaia data releases have seen the construction of many open cluster catalogues containing thousands of open clusters. Simulations of these clusters are needed in order to interpret observations, both existing and upcoming. M67 is an ideal open cluster to calibrate these simulations due to its advanced age and large, diverse binary populations. Moreover it is one of the most extensively observed open clusters with observations in several wavelengths. We aim to reproduce the global cluster properties of M67 with modern $N$-body simulations, as well as comparing its observed properties in the largest homogeneous open cluster catalogue with other available observations. We carry out several NBODY6++GPU simulations with varying initial conditions, including metallicity, half-mass radius, and the distribution of orbital binary parameters. Our models broadly reproduce the observed global properties of M67, and we are able to recreate the cluster's surface brightness profile, radial mass profile, and colour-magnitude diagram. Our favoured model indicates an initial half-mass radius of around 1.6 pc, although its total observable cluster mass may be too high. Further simulations are planned for a subsequent study, with a focus on recreating the present-day binary populations of M67.

title: Resolving the AGN Feeding and Feedback Cycle with ALMA2040
comment: Part of the ALMA2040 White Paper Series. 10 pages, 4 Figures
summary: Understanding how supermassive black holes (SMBHs) grow and regulate the growth of their host galaxies requires tracing the cold molecular interstellar medium (ISM) throughout the full AGN feeding-feedback cycle. Molecular gas constitutes both the primary fuel for star formation and black-hole accretion and one of the ISM phases most directly affected by AGN-driven radiation, winds, and radio jets. Over the past decade, ALMA has resolved circumnuclear molecular discs, rings, spirals, tori, and jet-driven outflows on scales of tens of parsecs in nearby AGN. These studies have demonstrated that combining spatially resolved gas kinematics with multi-line diagnostics is essential for disentangling the physical processes underlying the observed gas conditions. However, our current picture remains largely based on a limited number of exceptionally nearby systems. Most local AGN have instead been observed with ALMA in a single transition at moderate or low angular resolution, preventing a systematic characterisation of both the dynamics and physical state of the gas. Moreover, existing studies have largely overlooked kinetic-mode AGN hosted by massive early-type galaxies, despite their central importance for understanding maintenance-mode feedback. In this White Paper, we argue that ALMA2040 should transform these detailed case studies into a statistical framework. A $\sim10\times$ improvement in line sensitivity relative to the current ALMA, together with fast mosaicking, ultra-wide instantaneous bandwidth, and longer baselines (resolving up to $\sim9$ mas at 230 GHz), will enable homogeneous, multi-line mapping of the molecular ISM on giant molecular clouds scales across statistically significant samples of both radiative- and kinetic-mode AGN out to $z\lesssim0.1$.

title: The environments forming stellar and planetary systems
comment: 10 pages + 1 page affiliations, 1 figure, ALMA2040 whitepaper
summary: How does a star's birth environment set the mass, angular momentum and chemical complexity delivered to its planet-forming disk, and thereby whether it builds planets, brown dwarfs or stellar companions? This requires following material from the cloud to the sub-au to few-au scales where infalling gas, magnetized winds and the disk interact, across all star-forming environments. At frequencies where young disks are optically thin, current facilities, even ALMA after its Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade, fall short by a factor of a few in angular resolution and an order of magnitude in sensitivity. Likewise, resolving how disks around distant high-mass stars fragment into tight multiples requires a linear resolution of a few to a few tens of au, currently out of reach. Yet the disks characterized so far lie almost exclusively in nearby, isolated clouds at near-solar metallicity, although the environment (radiation field, ionization rate, gas and stellar density, pressure and metallicity) varies by orders of magnitude across the Galaxy. Most stars, probably including the Sun, form in clustered regions at kpc distances, and the widest metallicity range lies farther still, in the outer Galaxy, the Central Molecular Zone and the Magellanic Clouds. With three times finer angular resolution and ten times the sensitivity, ALMA2040 will follow the path of material from cloud to disk across the full stellar-mass spectrum and, for the first time, measure how this path changes with environment: resolving the sub-au infall-impact and wind-launching zones nearby, disk fragmentation and the onset of multiplicity in distant high-mass regions, and disk formation at a few tenths of solar metallicity. It will thereby reveal the dust-obscured, embedded origins of planetary systems that optical and infrared facilities, including the ELT, see only once they emerge, and show how the birth environment shapes them.

title: Let Sleeping Stars Li: Mapping Turnoff Lithium, the Lithium Dip, & Testing Standard Model Predictions in GALAH DR4 Subgiants
comment: 37 Pages; 15 Figures; Submitted to ApJ; Data available upon request (smedile.1@osu.edu); comments welcome
summary: Lithium is an excellent tracer of stellar mixing. We reconstruct the end of the main sequence lithium depletion pattern using the GALAH DR4 3D-NLTE lithium dataset for 22,442 stars, complemented by masses and subgiant lithium dilution factors inferred from YREC stellar models. We recover the two canonical features seen in clusters: a cool plateau ($\mathrm{M_{[Fe/H]_{\odot}}} \sim 1.2 \mathrm{M_\odot}$) with a median $A(Li) = 2.42$, and a steep plunge into the lithium dip ($\mathrm{M_{[Fe/H]_{\odot}}} \sim 1.35 \mathrm{M_\odot}$) dominated by upper limits at $A(Li) < 1.5$. Above the dip, our data reveal a striking new pattern with a wide range of abundances. We argue this reflects severe rotationally induced mixing in most stars, with lithium preserved in a minority where gravitational settling suppresses mixing. Lithium depletion with intrinsic dispersion is universal across the sample. Predicted and observed dilution trends agree well below the dip. For higher-mass stars, dilution corrections agree with standard models, but our upper envelope lies below open cluster values. We attribute this to a shallower lithium preservation zone and further evidence for gravitational settling and radiative levitation. We detect lithium in $\approx25\%$ of dip stars, whereas clusters show none; neither blurring of a narrow mass feature nor binary contamination fully explains this. The cool plateau is 0.8 dex below the solar meteoritic value across a wide range of $[Fe/H]$. After accounting for pre-main sequence depletion, the plateau is elevated at $\geq [Fe/H]_{\odot}$, possibly evidence for lithium production.

title: Searching for Dwarf Novae in 47 Tucanae
summary: The globular cluster 47 Tucanae has 43 strong cataclysmic variable candidates, four of which are confirmed dwarf novae. Tidal capture theory predicts the existence of dozens of dwarf novae, suggesting more are undiscovered. Using 435 nm and 475 nm long exposure images from Hubble's ACS camera, we searched five epochs of archival Hubble images and did not find any variability at the scale of a dwarf nova eruption. We found 1 previously undiscovered variable object on the main sequence that could not be classified as a CV; the object experienced a change of approximately 0.3 Mag in 425 nm, and 0.2 mag in 635 nm over the course of 12 days. The lack of new CV detections in 47 Tucanae could be a result of the short timescale of the DN eruption, and a low observing probability. However, this null result may also support research suggesting most CVs in globular clusters are not dynamically formed, and tidal capture theory overestimates the detectable CV population.

title: Double Trouble: How Unresolved Spectroscopic Binary Stars Skew GALAH DR4 Stellar Parameters
summary: Unresolved binary stars introduce systematic biases in stellar parameter estimates when analysed assuming a single star. Using $\sim$917{,}000 spectra from the Galactic Archaeology with HERMES (GALAH) Data Release 4 (DR4), we develop a binary spectral model that fits each observed spectrum as the superposition of two synthetic spectra generated from the same model architecture used by GALAH DR4. These generative spectral models take as input: effective temperature ($T_\mathrm{eff}$), surface gravity ($\log g$), iron abundance ([Fe/H]), projected rotation velocity ($v \sin i$), microturbulence velocity ($v_\mathrm{mic}$), and radial velocity ($v_\mathrm{rad}$). In our binary model, $T_\mathrm{eff}$ and $\log g$ are not fitted directly but are instead interpolated from PARSEC isochrones based on stellar mass and age, under the assumption that both components formed contemporaneously with the same compositions. We fit for the primary and secondary masses, a common age and [Fe/H], as well as individual $v \sin i$, $v_\mathrm{mic}$, and $v_\mathrm{rad}$ for each component. After iterative optimization and conservative quality cuts to ensure robust detections, we identify $\sim$12{,}911 candidate binary systems. We quantify typical biases introduced by unresolved binarity: $T_\mathrm{eff}$ shifts of $-142$ to $+200$ K, $\log g$ shifts of $-0.070$ to $+0.35$ dex, and [Fe/H] shifts of $-0.055$ to $+0.13$ dex. Despite our conservative approach reducing the number of detections, we recover known trends of increasing binary fraction with higher primary mass and lower metallicity, thus reflecting the broad trends of binary populations. Accounting for unresolved binaries is essential for accurate stellar population modelling and for interpreting spectroscopic surveys--particularly in low-metallicity systems or populations with more massive stars.

title: Gaia in Technicolor. I. A Simple Variability-Encoded Color-Magnitude Diagram
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific
summary: The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram is one of the most important tools in stellar astrophysics. In its modern, empirical form as the Gaia color-magnitude diagram (CMD), each star is represented with a point determined from its time-averaged brightness and color. However, many stars are intrinsically variable, and the fixed-point representation ignores the variety of ways in which a star can vary. As a system pulsates, eclipses, is irradiated, erupts, or otherwise varies, it moves through the CMD along a trajectory whose size, slope, and shape are determined by the physics driving the brightness and color variability. Here we exploit the near-simultaneous, three-band, multi-epoch photometry (MEP) released for ~11.7 million sources in Gaia DR3 to construct a variability-encoded CMD (VECMD). In this updated take on the traditional CMD, each star is represented not by a point but by a linear segment approximating the path it traces in absolute magnitude and color as it varies. Because these trajectories are built from the raw epoch data, they are agnostic to period and do not require phase-folding. We show that radial-mode pulsators trace looped, Lissajous-like trajectories that can encode the phase lag between radius and temperature. The Hertzsprung bump is even visible in the CMD loops of some Cepheids. Variable binary systems can trace tight color-correlated lines and/or hooked paths. Accreting and dust-obscured systems trace long, high-amplitude tracks aligned with the outburst or reddening vector. Distinct regions of the VECMD are dominated by distinct trajectory morphologies. We argue that these trajectories are period-independent fingerprints well suited to machine learning classification, which we will pursue on the much larger epoch-photometry sample expected in Gaia DR4. Finally, we present a free app called IVECMD for finding, classifying, and analyzing variable stars in the VECMD.

title: Seeing Through the RFI Mask: DT-FISTA Inpainting of Pulsar Dynamic Spectra via Fourier Sparsity
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, comments welcome
summary: Radio frequency interference (RFI) frequently contaminates radio observations, and excising affected samples leaves masked regions in sampled images. Replacing masked samples with zero or the mean causes spectral leakage in Fourier-domain power representations. This contamination is particularly severe for modern pulsar scintillation studies, which rely on identifying and characterizing faint parabolic scintillation arcs in secondary spectra, the 2D power spectra of dynamic spectra. Scintillation arcs probe discrete scattering screens in the interstellar medium (ISM) and constrain their physical properties. However, leakage can obscure faint arcs whose power is often $<10^{-3}$ of the dominant pulsar signal power. Wiener inpainting can mitigate this leakage, but a dense implementation requires $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ memory and $\mathcal{O}(JN^2)$ time for $N$ pixels and $J$ iterations, which is computationally expensive for full-resolution spectra containing millions of pixels. We introduce the decreasing-threshold fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (DT-FISTA). Using a sparse Fourier representation, DT-FISTA initially estimates masked intensities from the strongest Fourier components and progressively refines them with weaker components as the soft threshold decreases. Nesterov momentum extrapolation accelerates these updates. Each iteration uses 2D fast Fourier transforms (FFT) and pointwise operations, requiring $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory. Tests on $300\times300$ pixel patches from Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) observations yield lower reconstruction errors than the dense Wiener implementation, with runtime and memory requirements reduced by factors $>10^3$. Applied to full-resolution dynamic spectra, DT-FISTA suppresses mask-induced artifacts and reveals previously obscured faint arcs, enabling efficient ISM studies.

title: Extended J-band spectroscopy of red supergiants: parameter identifiability and metallicity robustness
comment: Comments: 20 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Red supergiants (RSGs) provide a near-infrared metallicity diagnostic complementary to optical hot-supergiant spectroscopy, but their low-resolution extragalactic use requires tests of parameter identifiability and modelling robustness. We quantify the information content of extended J-band RSG spectra at R=2000 over 1.155-1.340 um and assess recovery of effective temperature, surface gravity, microturbulence, and metallicity. Using MARCS/TURBOSPECTRUM spectra and an emulator, we perform a six-node Fisher analysis and controlled mock experiments, and analyse 21 SpeX spectra of 20 RSG candidates towards Per OB1. All four parameters produce measurable responses, but only 8-10% of the raw metallicity information and 4-7% of the gravity information are independent of the other parameter directions. Extending beyond 1.22 um provides median fractions of 60% of the raw and 66% of the nuisance-orthogonal metallicity information. Gravity dominates the weakest Fisher mode, while its prior choice shifts association means by at most 0.03 dex. Matched mocks recover metallicity with an rms error of 0.04 dex. Standard continuum treatment biases solar-metallicity mocks by about -0.23 dex, reduced to about -0.01 dex by our adopted treatment. Plausible CNO mismatch adds a zero-point sensitivity of 0.04-0.05 dex, and regularised covariance changes association means by at most 0.03 dex. The preferred analysis gives a mean [Z] = -0.10 dex with a star-to-star dispersion of 0.09 dex. Extended low-resolution J-band spectra therefore yield recoverable metallicity and temperature constraints once continuum placement and weak parameter directions are controlled, although the absolute scale remains conditional on the adopted atmosphere and line-formation framework.

title: The GAGE survey. I. Deep multi-band stellar variability characterization and automated classification toward Baade's window
summary: Context. Long-term photometric surveys of the Galactic bulge are vital for characterizing its stellar populations and structure, providing a foundation for next-generation facilities. Aims. We present initial results of the GalActic bulGe with plEiadi (GAGE) project, focusing on variable star discovery in Baade's Window. Methods. Using archival DECam (ugriz) data on the Blanco 4-m Telescope spanning six years, we applied high-precision PSF photometry. We developed a pipeline combining Generalized Lomb-Scargle analysis and polynomial light-curve modelling to derive mean multi-band magnitudes and amplitudes. Results. Quality cuts yield 6,304 high-confidence variable sources. We expand multi-band coverage for 4,568 sources in common with OGLE IV and uncover 1,736 (~28%) new candidates absent from OGLE IV. Using a Random Forest classifier, we categorize these sources, finding that 1,391 were also missing from both Gaia DR3 and VVV. This population is concentrated at the fainter end (i >= 17.5 mag), enabled by our deeper detection limits. Conclusions. Our pipeline effectively probes deep, highly crowded fields, expanding the variable star inventory of the inner Galaxy as a benchmark for Rubin-LSST.

title: A Hectospec Spectroscopic Census of Kinematic Members in the Orion Nebula Cluster
comment: 23 pages, 15 figures and 10 tables (including tables in apenddices)
summary: We present a comprehensive spectroscopic census of the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC), based primarily on low-resolution optical spectroscopy obtained with MMT/Hectospec. We derive spectral types, youth indicators, and accretion diagnostics for 1513 stars located in the ONC region, enabling the identification and characterization of pre-main-sequence stars. We combine these measurements with a kinematic membership analysis based on Gaia Data Release 3 astrometry to identify and confirm cluster members. Using these combined diagnostics, we identify and characterize 780 bona fide T Tauri stars associated with the ONC. In addition, we construct a census of protoplanetary discs using infrared photometry obtained with the IRAC and MIPS instruments aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope. We further derive stellar masses, ages, and extinctions using the MassAge code, which combines photometric and spectroscopic inputs with stellar evolutionary models, and employs a Monte Carlo approach for uncertainty propagation. The resulting homogeneous catalogue of ONC members provides spectroscopic characterizations, kinematic membership constraints, disc diagnostics, and self-consistent estimates of stellar physical parameters. This dataset offers a refined view of the stellar population of the ONC and provides a robust foundation for investigating its kinematic structure, age distribution, and protoplanetary disc population.

title: Survey of Orion Disks with ALMA (SODA) IV: Millimeter variability of protoplanetary disks
comment: Accepted by A&A on 12/10/2026
summary: Context. Short-term millimeter-wavelength variability in Class II young stellar objects (YSOs) has been considered minimal, often dismissed as very rare in ALMA-based studies on short timescales. However, recent findings suggest that variability on sub-day timescales is significant. Aims. This study aims to quantify short timescale (~1 hour to ~3 days) millimeter flux variability in unresolved Class II YSO disks observed as part of the SODA survey, leveraging its large dataset to assess the statistical significance of such variability across the LDN 1641 and LDN 1647 regions in Orion. Methods. We analyze ALMA Band 6 observations of 873 YSOs obtained over multiple epochs using a custom flux extraction pipeline to separate individual execution blocks. By computing variability factors and statistical deviations from the mean flux, we identify sources exhibiting significant variability, accounting for noise and calibrator stability. Results. Even with conservative selection criteria, we identify 20 variable sources within the sample (~5.3% of all detections). The maximum of the measured variability factor is >=7 over about one hour. More liberal selection criteria yield up to 60 sources that could be called potentially variable (~15.9%). Conclusions. The number of variable sources detected in our sample indicates physical processes operating on time scales of hours, likely associated with magnetic reconnection and/or synchrotron radiation or strong cases of magnetic accretion changes. These detections show the need to reconsider typical stability assumptions in single-epoch observations and calls for follow-up studies in star-forming regions with ALMA. Masses derived from unresolved measurements could potentially be biased by this sort of variability.
